worlds.research_question: Determine why Battery Pack B shows faster capacity degradation than Battery Pack A under nominally identical fleet use, whether fast-charging exposure is the primary driver, and which competing explanations should be retained.

catalog.descriptor: Repeat matched degradation measurements under the same nominal operating conditions
Perturb one operating condition around the current fleet baseline
Test whether one simple proposed mechanism alone explains the pack difference
Run a controlled intervention on the suspected fast-charging factor
Inspect a boundary subgroup where the degradation gap may change
Audit reliability of capacity and degradation measurement
Run robustness checks under alternative exclusions and matching rules

modules.J4: Across 14 matched monthly intervals, Pack B loses usable capacity 1.8 to 3.1 percentage points faster than Pack A. Pack B was already about 0.5 percentage points worse before the newest charging policy was introduced.
modules.Q8: Under matched temperature and trip-length strata, the degradation gap ranges from 0.8 to 2.7 percentage points and is largest in high-depth-of-discharge use.
modules.B3: Pack B vehicles have more high-mileage prior service and more frequent overnight low-state-of-charge periods. Matching these histories reduces the estimated pack gap by about 0.6 percentage points.
modules.T6: During four months when fast charging was rare in both fleets, Pack B still degraded about 1.1 percentage points faster. Fast-charging exposure alone therefore does not explain the full difference.
modules.M1: A randomized charging crossover on 120 matched vehicles found that reducing fast-charging exposure lowered six-month capacity loss by 0.9 percentage points, 95% CI 0.3 to 1.5.
modules.X7: The pack difference is near zero in low-mileage vehicles but reaches 3 to 4 percentage points in high-mileage vehicles with frequent deep discharge.
modules.D5: Independent capacity tests agree with onboard estimates with ICC 0.95. A calibration audit found one firmware version in Pack B underestimates state of health by about 0.3 percentage points.
modules.H2: After excluding the affected firmware, matching prior mileage, and varying degradation definitions, the fast-charging effect remains 0.6 to 1.1 points while a residual Pack B disadvantage of 0.7 to 1.6 points persists.

worlds.research_question: Determine why Distribution Center B has a higher parcel-damage rate than Center A, whether conveyor speed is the primary driver, and which competing explanations should be retained.

catalog.descriptor: Run a controlled intervention on the suspected conveyor-speed factor
Audit reliability of damage detection and classification
Perturb one operating condition around the current handling baseline
Run robustness checks under alternative exclusions and matching rules
Repeat matched damage measurements under the same nominal operating conditions
Test whether one simple proposed mechanism alone explains the center difference
Inspect a boundary subgroup where the damage gap may change

modules.C7: Across 16 matched weeks, Center B has a parcel-damage rate 1.9 to 3.4 percentage points above Center A. Center B was already about 0.6 points worse before the latest conveyor-speed setting was introduced.
modules.A5: Under matched parcel size, packaging class, and shift load, the center gap ranges from 0.9 to 3.0 points and is largest during high-throughput periods.
modules.R3: Center B has more temporary workers and more frequent shift handovers. Matching worker tenure and handover frequency reduces the estimated center gap by about 0.7 percentage points.
modules.V4: On five shifts when both centers ran at the same slower conveyor speed, Center B still had a damage rate about 1.2 points higher. Conveyor speed alone does not explain the full difference.
modules.F2: A randomized speed crossover on 3,000 parcels found that reducing conveyor speed lowered damage by 0.8 percentage points, 95% CI 0.3 to 1.3.
modules.L9: The center gap is near zero for rigid boxed goods but 3 to 5 points for fragile items requiring multi-stage transfer.
modules.P8: Independent inspectors agree on damage classification 95% of the time. An audit found Center B camera placement misses some minor damage and biases automated rates downward by about 0.2 points.
modules.N1: After matching workforce tenure, excluding ambiguous camera cases, and varying damage definitions, the speed effect remains 0.5 to 1.0 points while a residual Center B disadvantage of 0.8 to 1.7 points persists.
